# Faster Exact Algorithms for Equal-Subset-Sum

Ryosuke Yamano<sup>∗</sup>

Tetsuo Shibuya<sup>†</sup>

**Abstract**

We study exact algorithms for Equal-Subset-Sum in the worst-case setting: given a set _S_ of _n_ integers, find two distinct subsets \(A,B\subseteq S\) whose sums are equal. We establish a new state- of-the-art bound for this problem by improving the fastest known algorithm, due to Randolph and We\(\unknown\)rzycki (S 2026), from _O_<sup>∗</sup>(1.7067_<sup>n</sup>_) time and space to an algorithm that runs in _O_<sup>∗</sup>(1.6994_<sup>n</sup>_) time and uses _O_<sup>∗</sup>(1.5664_<sup>n</sup>_) space. We also improve the best known polynomial- space running time, due to Mucha, Nederlof, Pawlewicz, and W\(\unknown\)rzycki (ESA 2019), from _O_<sup>∗</sup>(2.6817_<sup>n</sup>_) to _O_<sup>∗</sup>(2.5430_<sup>n</sup>_). Finally, we investigate time-space tradeoffs for this problem and improve the running times achievable under a broad range of exponential-space bounds.

## 1 Introduction

Subset-Sum is a fundamental NP-hard problem, which can be formulated as follows.

**Problem 1.1** (Subset-Sum)**.** Given a multiset _S_ of _n_ integers and a target integer _t_, output a subset \(A\subseteq S\) such that \(t=\sum_{a\in A}a\), if such a subset exists.

Subset-Sum admits a simple meet-in-the-middle algorithm, due to Horowitz and Sahni \[19\], that runs in _O_<sup>∗</sup>(2<sup>_n/_2</sup>) time <sup>1</sup>. This remains the standard running-time bound for exact algorithms for Subset-Sum, and the fastest known algorithm \[13\] improves over the _O_(2<sup>_n/_2</sup>) bound only by a polynomial factor. Whether there exists an algorithm for Subset-Sum that runs in \(O^*(2^{(0.5-\delta)n})\) time for some constant \(\delta>0\) remains a long-standing open question.

Closely related to this open problem, Howgrave-Graham and Joux \[20\] broke this meet-in-the- middle barrier in the _average-case_ setting by giving an _O_<sup>∗</sup>(2<sup>0.337_n_</sup>)-time algorithm, which was later improved to _O_<sup>∗</sup>(2<sup>0.283_n_</sup>) by \[8, 9\]. The algorithm of Howgrave-Graham and Joux introduced the representation technique, which was later also used for Equal-Subset-Sum (ESS), an important variant of Subset-Sum that can be formulated as follows.

**Problem 1.2** (Equal-Subset-Sum (ESS) \[31\])**.** Given a set _S_ of _n_ integers, output two distinct subsets \(A,B\subseteq S\) such that \(\sum_{a\in A}a=\sum_{b\in B}b\), if such subsets exist.

ESS admits a simple meet-in-the-middle algorithm that runs in _O_<sup>∗</sup>(3<sup>_n/_2</sup>) time. Surprisingly, the authors of \[25\] broke this meet-in-the-middle barrier for ESS in the _worst-case_ setting by exploiting the representation technique, giving an algorithm that runs in _O_<sup>∗</sup>(1.7088_<sup>n</sup>_) time and space. In the _average-case_ setting, the authors of \[12\] gave an \(O^*(3^{0.387n})\le O^*(1.5299^n)\)-time algorithm for ESS. The open question of whether the running time for ESS in the worst-case setting can be improved beyond _O_<sup>∗</sup>(1.7088_<sup>n</sup>_) \[21, Section 5, Question 1\] was answered affirmatively very recently by Randolph and Węgrzycki \[28\], who gave an algorithm that runs in _O_<sup>∗</sup>(1.7067_<sup>n</sup>_) time and space.

### 1.1 Our Results

In this work, we focus on exact algorithms for ESS in the worst-case setting. All our algorithms are Monte Carlo algorithms that never return false positives, and their error probabilities can be reduced to \(2^{-\Omega(n)}\) by repetition. Our first result establishes a new state-of-the-art algorithm for ESS by further improving the result of \[28\]. While the running-time improvement is our primary contribution, the algorithm also reduces the space usage by a much larger exponential factor.

**Theorem 1.3.** _There exists a Monte Carlo algorithm for ESS that runs in O_<sup>∗</sup>(1.6994_<sup>n</sup>_) _time and uses O_<sup>∗</sup>(1.5664_<sup>n</sup>_) _space._

Our second result improves the polynomial-space running time for ESS. We improve upon the _O_<sup>∗</sup>(2.6817_<sup>n</sup>_)-time algorithm of \[25\] by analyzing two approaches suited to different parameter regimes: one based on recent improvements for low-space Element Distinctness \[11\], and the other using the fast polynomial-space Subset-Sum algorithm of \[5\] as a subroutine.

**Theorem 1.4.** _There exists a Monte Carlo algorithm for ESS that runs in O_<sup>∗</sup>(2.5430_<sup>n</sup>_) _time and uses polynomial space._

For Subset-Sum, Schroeppel and Shamir \[29\] gave a time-space tradeoff _T=O_<sup>∗</sup>(2_<sup>n</sup>/S_<sup>2</sup>) for any space bound \(S\le O^*(2^{n/4})\). This tradeoff was later improved for almost all choices of the tradeoff parameter by \[3\]. In contrast, for ESS, the analogous Schroeppel–Shamir-type tradeoff,<tbc>

## 1.2 Our Main Techniques

The algorithms of \[25\] focus on the solution size \(\ell=|A|+|B|\), where _A_ and _B_ form a disjoint solution of ESS. They gave an algorithm that runs in \(O^*(2^\ell)\) time and space for \(\ell>n/2\), which is fast when \(\ell\) is small. In our algorithm, we introduce a simple random modification to the input instance; see Algorithm 1 in Section 3. This modification reduces the solution size \(\ell\) with inverse-exponential probability. Although we need to pay an additional exponential cost to successfully reduce \(\ell\), the exponential speedup obtained from the reduction in \(\ell\) dominates this cost in the bottleneck case \(\ell\approx 0.773n\) of \[25\]. ### 1.3 Related Works

The recent attention to exact algorithms for ESS has also led to improvements for the closely related Pigeonhole ESS problem \[27\], a constrained variant of ESS in which all input integers are positive and their sum is at most 2_<sup>n</sup>_-2. By the pigeonhole principle, a solution is guaranteed to exist. Thus, Pigeonhole ESS is a _total search problem_, and it has also been studied in the TFNP context \[4, 30\]. Pigeonhole ESS admits a meet-in-the-middle-based algorithm that runs in _O_<sup>∗</sup>(2<sup>_n/_2</sup>) time, which was recently improved to _O_<sup>∗</sup>(2<sup>_n/_3</sup>) time \[22, 21\].

A natural optimization variant of ESS is the Subset-Sum-Ratio problem \[31\], in which the task is to find two disjoint subsets whose sums have ratio as close to 1 as possible. A 1.324-approximation algorithm was given in \[31\], and the first FPTAS for the problem was given in \[6\]. This FPTAS was later simplified in \[26\]. Subsequent works improved the running time \[24, 2, 10\].

ESS also has connections to computational biology \[16, 14\]. The authors of \[15\] considered _k_-ESS, in which the task is to find _k_ disjoint subsets whose sums are all equal. Other variants of ESS were studied in \[17\], which also established their NP-hardness.

## 2 Preliminaries

We use the asymptotic notation \(O^*(\cdot)\), \(\Omega^*(\cdot)\), and \(\Theta^*(\cdot)\) to suppress polynomial factors in _n_, where _n_ denotes the number of integers in an ESS instance. More precisely, _f(n_)=_O_<sup>∗</sup>(_g(n_)) if \(f(n)\le g(n)\cdot n^{O(1)}\), and \(f(n)=\Omega^*(g(n))\) if \(f(n)\ge g(n)\cdot n^{-O(1)}\). We write \(f(n)=\Theta^*(g(n))\) if both _f(n_)=_O_<sup>∗</sup>(_g(n_)) and \(f(n)=\Omega^*(g(n))\) hold. Throughout the paper, all logarithms are base 2. The binary entropy function is defined by _H(x_)=-_x_log_x_-(1-_x_)log(1-_x_) for \(x\in(0,1)\), with _H_(0)=_H_(1)=0. We write \[_n_\] to denote the set {1_,...,n_}. For a set of integers _T_, we write \(\sum(T)=\sum_{t\in T}t\) for its sum. For integers _p_, _u_, and _v_, we write \(u\equiv_pv\) to denote \(u\equiv v(modp)\). We denote by \(X\Delta Y\) the symmetric difference of two sets _X_ and _Y_ ; that is, \(X\Delta Y=(X\backslash Y)\cup(Y\backslash X)\).

By Monte Carlo algorithms, we mean randomized algorithms that may produce only false negatives with constant probability. The error probability can be reduced to \(2^{-\Omega(n)}\) by repeating the algorithm poly(_n_) times, without affecting the running times expressed using \(O^*(\cdot)\) notation. We frequently use the following well-known inequalities.

**Fact 2.1.** _For any integers n and x with_ \(0\le x\le n\)_, we have_ \(\frac{1}{n+1}2^{H(x/n)n}\le\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{x}\le 2^{H(x/n)n}\)_. In particular,_ \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{x}=\Theta^*(2^{H(x/n)n})\).

We may also use the following fact to remove floors and ceilings in the \(O^*(\cdot)\) notation.

**Fact 2.2** (\[32, eq.(4)\])**.** _For any_ \(x,y\in[0,1]\)_, we have_ \(|H(x)-H(y)|\le H(|x-y|)\)_. Consequently, if_ \(x,y\in[0,1]\) _satisfy_ \(|x-y|\le O(1/n)\)_, then_ \(|H(x)-H(y)|\le O((logn)/n)\).

We adopt the input assumptions from \[25\]: the input set _S_ consists of positive integers and satisfies \(\sum(S)\le 2^{O(n)}\). We enforce these assumptions using the following preprocessing lemma, which is based on \[25, Appendix A of the full version\]. For completeness, we provide a proof in Appendix A of this paper.

**Lemma 2.3.** _Given a set S of n integers satisfying_ \(|s|\le 2^m\) _for all_ \(s\in S\)_, the following holds. If_ \(0\in S\) _or_ \(m\ge 2^n\)_, then ESS on S can be solved in O_(poly(_n,m_)) _time. Otherwise, with probability at least_ 1-_O_(2<sup>-_n_</sup>)_, we can construct, in O_(poly(_n,m_)) _time, a set_ \(S'\) _of_ \(n+\lceil logn\rceil\) _positive integers satisfying_ \(0<s'\le 2^{O(n)}\) _for all_ \(s'\in S'\)_, and satisfying the following properties: if_ \(S'\) _has no ESS solution, then neither does S; conversely, from any ESS solution of_ \(S'\)_, we can reconstruct a corresponding ESS solution of S in O_(poly(_n,m_)) _time._

Lemma 2.3 increases the input size by only _O_(log_n_). Thus, a running time of the form \(O^*(2^{\Theta(n)})\) changes only by a factor of 2<sup>_O_(log_n_)</sup>=poly(_n_), which is absorbed in the \(O^*(\cdot)\) notation.

For simplicity, we also assume that _n_ is divisible by 12. This can be achieved by setting \(M=\sum(S)+1\) and adding _O_(1) elements of the form _M,_2_M,_4_M,_8_M,..._ to _S_. We define a minimum solution as follows.

**Definition 2.4** (Minimum solution)**.** For an ESS instance with input set _S_, a solution \(A,B\subseteq S\) is called a minimum solution if |_A_|+|_B_| is minimized. We refer to the value |_A_|+|_B_| as the minimum solution size, denoted by \(\ell\), and define the minimum solution ratio as \(\ell'=\ell/n\).

By trying all possible values \(\ell\in[n]\), we incur only a polynomial overhead. If no execution finds a solution, then the algorithm reports that the instance is a No instance. Thus, in the following, we may assume that the minimum solution size \(\ell\) is given in advance.

When analyzing the bounds in terms of the minimum solution ratio \(\ell'\), we may upper-bound the running time and space usage by maximizing over the continuous interval (0,1\], instead of the discrete set {1_/n,_2_/n,...,(n_-1)_/n,_1} of possible values of \(\ell'\).

## 3 Faster Exponential-Space Algorithm

We first describe a modification of the input instance that may reduce the number of integers required to represent a solution. The algorithm randomly selects a subset of the input integers, partitions them into disjoint pairs, and replaces each pair with its sum and difference, as shown in Algorithm 1. In Lemma 3.1, we show that an ESS solution for the modified instance can be transformed into a valid ESS solution for the original instance under a certain condition.

Suppose that_ \(S'\) _admits an ESS solution_ \(A',B'\subseteq S'\) _with_ \(A'\cap B'=\emptyset\)_. If _x<sub>i</sub>+y<sub>i</sub>_ belongs to the solution, then we replace it by _x<sub>i</sub>_ and _y<sub>i</sub>_ in the same subset. If _x<sub>i</sub>-y<sub>i</sub>_ belongs to the solution, then we replace it by _x<sub>i</sub>_ in the same subset and place _y<sub>i</sub>_ in the other subset. Observe that these transformations preserve the equality of the subset sums. Applying this transformation independently to every obtained pair yields a valid ESS solution for the original instance _S_. Since the number of obtained pairs is at most _n/_2 and each pair is processed using only a constant number of arithmetic operations, the reconstruction procedure runs in polynomial time.

By Lemma 2.3, all input integers are positive, and thus _x<sub>i</sub>+y<sub>i</sub>\>x<sub>i</sub>-y<sub>i</sub>_ for every obtained pair (_x<sub>i</sub>,y<sub>i</sub>_). In this case, the corresponding elements immediately yield a valid ESS solution for the original instance by Lemma 3.1, and thus the algorithm may terminate early. Therefore, in the following, we assume that no value collisions occur in the modified instance, and hence \(|S|=|S'|\).

Moreover, the input assumption imposed by Lemma 2.3 continues to hold, since all generated integers remain positive and are at most twice the maximum value in the original input set _S_.

## 4 Faster Polynomial-Space Algorithm

For algorithms restricted to poly(_n_) space, we can employ the low-space element distinctness algorithm. This algorithm was introduced in \[7\], generalized in \[5\], and later freed from non-standard assumptions in \[11, 23\]. Lemma 4.1 can be inferred from \[11, Section 4.2, proof of Theorem 1.1\]. The same extracted lemma is also stated in \[22, Theorem 12\].

**Lemma 4.1** (\[11\])**.** _Given random access to an array of N nonnegative integers a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>N</sub>, with_ \(a_i\le poly(N)\) _for all_ \(i\in[N]\)_, suppose that the array contains at least one colliding pair, that is, a pair_ (_i,j_) _with_ \(i\neq j\) _and a<sub>i</sub>=a<sub>j</sub>. Then there is a Monte Carlo algorithm that reports such a pair using only_ polylog(_N_) _space and_

\(O\left(\frac{N\sqrt{F_2}}{F_2-N}polog(N)\right)\)

_time, where_ \(F_2=\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N\mathbf{1}[a_i=a_j]\) _is the second frequency moment. In particular, under the above assumption,_ \(F_2\in[N+2,N^2]\).

Although the statement in \[11\] is phrased for positive integers, the same bound applies to nonnegative integers by adding 1 to every array entry, which preserves all collisions. We apply Lemma 4.1 to the 2_<sup>n</sup>_ subset sums of _S_ to obtain Theorem 4.2.

**Theorem 4.2.** _Let_ \(\ell'\) _be the minimum solution ratio. Then there is a Monte Carlo algorithm for ESS that runs in_ \(O^*(2^{(\ell^\prime+1/2)n})\) _time using polynomial space._

_Proof._ We provide random access to the list _L_ of all subset sums of _S_={_w_<sub>1</sub>_,...,w<sub>n</sub>_} by computing each element on the fly. Specifically, for each index \(i\in[N]\), where _N_=2_<sup>n</sup>_, let

\(X_i=\{j\in[n]|\text{the}j\text{-th least significant bit of the binary representation of}i-1\text{is}1\}.\)

Then the _i_-th element of _L_ is computed as \(L_i=\sum_{j\in X_i}w_j\). This gives random access to _L_ using polylog(_N_) time and space. We apply Lemma 4.1 to _L_. A colliding pair in _L_ corresponds exactly to two distinct subsets of _S_ with equal sum, and hence yields an ESS solution.

It remains to bound the running time. Let \(A,B\subseteq S\) be a minimum solution, so that \(|A\cup B|=\ell'n\). Let \(Z=S\backslash(A\cup B)\); then \(|Z|=(1-\ell')n\). For every subset \(Z'\subseteq Z\), the two subsets \(A\cup Z'\) and \(B\cup Z'\) have equal sum. Therefore, these pairs contribute at least \(2^{|Z|}=2^{(1-\ell^\prime)n}\) nontrivial terms to _F_<sub>2</sub>, and hence \(F_2\ge N+2^{(1-\ell^\prime)n}\). Since the function \(\sqrt{x}/(x-N)\) is monotonically decreasing for \(x\in[N+2,N^2]\), we can upper-bound the running time by setting \(F_2=N+2^{(1-\ell^\prime)n}\). Thus,

\(O\left(\frac{N\sqrt{F_2}}{F_2-N}polog(N)\right)\le O\left(\frac{2^n\sqrt{2^n+2^{(1-\ell^\prime)n}}}{2^{(1-\ell^\prime)n}}poly(n)\right)\le O^*(2^{(\ell^\prime+1/2)n}).\)

Hence, the algorithm runs in \(O^*(2^{(\ell^\prime+1/2)n})\) time and uses polynomial space.

A fast polynomial-space algorithm for the Subset-Sum problem was given in \[5\], and the non- standard assumptions used in its analysis were later removed in \[11\].

**Lemma 4.3** (\[5, 11\])**.** _There is a Monte Carlo algorithm for Subset Sum that runs in O_<sup>∗</sup>(2<sup>0.86_n_</sup>) _time using polynomial space._

We use the polynomial-space algorithm for the Subset Sum problem as a subroutine to prove Theorem 4.4.

**Theorem 4.4.** _Let_ \(\ell'\) _be the minimum solution ratio. Then there is a Monte Carlo algorithm for ESS that runs in_ \(O^*(2^{(H(\ell^\prime)+0.86\ell^\prime)n})\) _time using polynomial space._

_Proof._ Let \(\ell=\ell'n\) be the minimum solution size. We iterate over all subsets \(X\subseteq S\) of size \(\ell\), keeping only the current subset in memory. For each such subset _X_, if \(\sum(X)\) is odd, then _X_ cannot be partitioned into two subsets of equal sum, so we skip this case. Otherwise, we run the polynomial-space Subset-Sum algorithm of Lemma 4.3 on the instance _X_ with target \(\sum(X)/2\).

Since there exists a minimum ESS solution \(A,B\subseteq S\) such that \(|A|+|B|=\ell\) and \(A\cap B=\emptyset\), the iteration eventually considers \(X=A\cup B\), and the corresponding Subset-Sum instance with target \(\sum(X)/2\) has a solution. The running time is therefore

\(O^*\left(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{\ell}2^{0.86\ell}\right)\le O^*(2^{(H(\ell^\prime)+0.86\ell^\prime)n}).\)

The space usage remains polynomial, since we iterate over the subsets _X_ one by one while storing only the current subset, and each call to the Subset-Sum algorithm uses polynomial space.
